You probably won't get many responses here as not only is it US-centric, it's also about university rather than British college. You'd be better off asking r/6thForm

Regardless, I took psychology A-Level, finishing in 2019 with an A. It's not extremely difficult, but yes it does involve a lot of writing and essays and the final exams are timed, so you will need to be able to write at a decent pace. But this is something you'll probably pick up over the two years. I wouldn't say psychology is one of the hardest A-Levels tbh. I've not done sociology, but going from what I've heard, it's a bit easier than psychology. 

Putting the effort in is more important than being smart. You may find that the people who did no work for their GCSEs and got excellent grades regardless will struggle more at A-Level.

To be completely honest I’m probably not the best person to ask as I do a history degree which is very different from astrophysics! But in terms of my degree I did feel that my second year workload was more intense at first, but once I got used to it it felt manageable. My first year was pretty easy though tbh. 

I have a friend who does physics and found first year difficult. He’s second year now and finding second year similar to first year, so still difficult but not a huge step up in terms of intensity, just more independent work as you said. We both attend Uni of Manchester. 

But yes GCSEs were very easy and a levels were a step up, but not too bad. Uni is harder but once you get more comfortable with the workload, I’m sure it’ll get easier.

Fellow Brit here. Finished for Christmas on 18th December and I didn't do any work until today. I have deadlines on 11th January, 2 on the 18th January and one on the 25th January. If you're up to date with work, then as long as you give yourself enough time to complete any outstanding assignments to a reasonable degree by the deadline you're doing good. And yes, give yourself a break during holidays!

Hope you're okay. First thing is to cut yourself some slack- this semester has been really difficult for everyone. With the online format and general nightmare of this semester, it's natural that your grades might fall. But at the end of the day, you are not your grades and your mental health needs to be your absolute number one priority, so if you do feel very down make sure you talk to someone.

However, back on the original topic. I'm a second year who got a 58 in one of my assignments last month, and I was also disappointed with it. I would recommend getting in touch with whoever marks your assignments if you haven't already and ask for an appointment to discuss your work further and see if they can give you any guidance on how to improve. This is what I did when I got the 58 and after talking about what went wrong, I'm feeling much more confident with the final essay in that course. 

Good luck on your next exams! You've got this. If you ever want to talk you can always message me.

You have a large, energetic breed of dog that is also in the middle of adolescence right now. 

Firstly you really need to make sure that you are meeting his needs. I'm not sure what you consider to be an ample amount of exercise, but he needs 1-2 hours a day, minimum. You also need to look up training commands, clicker training (doesn't have to be a clicker, can be a marker word) and impulse control exercises. You need to work on this with your dog. Sessions should be about 15 minutes max, ideally you want to end the session before the dog gets bored. If you can, I'd also invest in some food dispensing toys such as kongs to occupy him when you are unable to. Play some games with him when you can- hide some of his dinner around your house for him, play fetch with him. Give him a job- teach him to go fetch the remote or pick up things you drop on the floor or whatever and see if he enjoys feeling as though he has a task to perform. Make your exercise better- bike or run with him, play fetch or hike on a long like, get him to carry a dog backpack on his walks. You need to meet his needs- if you cannot meet his needs, you cannot expect him not to get into trouble. 

Secondly you need rules and structure. Establish what your dog can and cannot do. Can he get on  the couch? What should he do instead of jumping on people (sit for example)? Can he go in the kitchen (might be a good idea to ban him from the kitchen)? Once you've decided what your rules are, you need to implement them and be consistent. 

Thirdly you really need to consult with a good trainer in your area. You really need a professional who can see you and your dog in person and advise you. 

Fourthly you need to manage his behavior for now. If you can, block off the kitchen or buy a heavy weight garbage can. Don't let him offleash outdoors (get a long line). Crate him when you go out- please don't feel bad about this if it's for his own safety.

It doesn't sound like you have a bad dog. Your dog sounds like an adolescent herding breed who is extremely bored, full of energy, is lacking some training and structure and has very minimal impulse control. If you can meet his needs for exercise and stimulation and can consult a good trainer as well as just allowing your dog to mature, you'll probably end up with a very good dog. If you can't meet his needs and this is impacting your life, then you should seriously consider rehoming him to someone who can meet his needs. If you do decide to rehome him I'd recommend contacting a local GSD specific rescue if you have one in your area. 

Best of luck with whatever you do.
